body.heading: A cone full of courage
paragraphs: In Germany, Austria, and parts of Switzerland, children starting school receive a Schultüte — a large, decorated cone filled with sweets, small school supplies, and treats. The tradition is about two centuries old, and its purpose is transparent and kind: to sweeten a day that is exciting and frightening in roughly equal measure.
The cone is often made by parents or crafted at kindergarten, carried proudly for the photograph, and opened — by long-standing rule — only once the child gets home.

body.heading: Other ways to soften a threshold
paragraphs: Many families mark the first day more simply: a special breakfast, a photograph by the same front door every year, a note in the lunchbox, the walk to school taken slowly with a favourite person. In Japan, the entrance ceremony is a formal occasion, and the sturdy randoseru backpack a child receives is expected to last all six years of elementary school.
What the customs share is the message: this threshold matters, we see you crossing it, and the family is on both sides of it with you.

body.heading: Start small and repeat yearly
paragraphs: A first-day tradition needs only to be small enough to survive a busy September: the same breakfast, the same photo spot, the same question at dinner — 'tell us one thing'. Repeated, it becomes the measuring wall against which childhood is quietly recorded.
Ask older relatives how their first day was marked, in their country and their time. School thresholds are a fine excuse to collect family history.

description: Germany's sweet-filled Schultüte and Japan's entrance ceremonies mark the first day of school as a threshold worth celebrating kindly.
